title: Just bury your trash - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Modern engineered landfill is cheaper and environmentally cleaner than most recycling, and the energy math on reusable substitutes (cotton bags need 173 reuses, ceramic mugs 1,000) rarely works; the only clearly justified recycling stream is metals, where aluminum saves up to 95 percent of energy versus virgin production. Recycling mid-grade plastic implies a carbon abatement cost above $1,000 per ton versus roughly $490 per ton for direct air capture, so waste-policy money is being spent at several times the market rate for CO2 removal.

insights.claim: A conventional cotton shopping bag must be reused 173 times before it beats a single-use polyethylene bag on environmental cost, according to Britain's Environment Agency, with Denmark's equivalent body estimating a similar ratio.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Regulatory bans on single-use plastic packaging may raise, not lower, lifecycle footprint — a compliance-cost risk for retailers and an opening for plastics producers to contest the science.
insights.quote: a conventional cotton bag needed to be reused 173 times to beat plastic
insights.locator: Producing tiny slivers of plastic

insights.claim: Making the polyethylene resin for one thin plastic bag and blowing and sealing it consumes about 0.6 megajoules, versus roughly 1,725 megajoules for a cotton bag — about 3,050 times as much energy — because cotton bags weigh around 200 grams against eight grams for polyethylene and require spinning, weaving, drying, sizing, dyeing, and finishing.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The energy gap between petro-plastics and natural-fiber substitutes is three orders of magnitude, so any 'green substitution' investment thesis must be underwritten on actual reuse counts, not material sentiment.
insights.quote: Making the polyethylene resin for a single thin plastic bag, then blowing and sealing it, uses something like 0.6 megajoules, roughly the same energy as a kettle uses for forty seconds.
insights.locator: Producing tiny slivers of plastic

insights.claim: A steel straw uses 10 grams of steel against 0.2 grams of plastic for a disposable straw, requiring 150 reuses to break even on resources even before accounting for the energy of hot-water washing.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Durable-goods substitutes carry a large embodied-energy debt that consumer behavior rarely repays; treat 'sustainable' consumer-products branding as unverified until reuse rates are disclosed.
insights.quote: it would take 150 reuses for a steel straw to use fewer resources than a plastic one. And who would go without washing it?
insights.locator: The same pattern shows up almost everywhere

insights.claim: A ceramic mug only beats a polystyrene cup on energy after 1,000 uses and only with an efficient dishwasher, while a returnable milk bottle needs roughly ten or more trips to beat a polyethylene carton and cloth diapers come out roughly tied with disposables once cotton, laundering, hot water, and detergent are counted.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The recurring pattern — reuse wins only at high cycle counts with efficient washing — is a transferable screen for evaluating any circular-economy business model's real environmental claim.
insights.quote: A ceramic mug only beats a polystyrene cup on energy use after 1,000 uses, and even then only if your dishwasher is fairly efficient. Run a less efficient one and the disposable cup wins on energy forever.
insights.locator: The same pattern shows up almost everywhere

themes.theme: Metals are the only clear recycling win

insights.claim: Recycling one kilogram of steel saves 1.4 kilograms of iron ore and 65 percent of the energy, while aluminum recycling can save as much as 95 percent, because virgin metal requires energy-intensive chemical reduction of ores whereas recycling is mostly remelting elemental metal.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Secondary-metal capacity (scrap-fed EAF steel, secondary aluminum) has a structural energy-cost advantage that survives any change in recycling policy — the durable part of the circular-economy trade.
insights.quote: For aluminum, the energy savings from recycling can be as high as 95 percent.
insights.locator: The case for recycling to avoid using

insights.claim: About 30 percent of the metal used in global steel production is already recycled scrap, driven by the fact that recycling metal is cheaper than mining, refining, and smelting — not by mandates.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Where recycling is genuinely economic it already happens at scale without subsidy; policy-driven recycling volumes should therefore be read as a signal of negative unit economics.
insights.quote: About 30 percent of the metal used in steel production globally is now recycled scrap.
insights.locator: The case for recycling to avoid using

insights.claim: Copper, cobalt, lithium, and nickel justify recycling not because global reserves are running out but because copper ore grades are declining as the best deposits are depleted, and because cobalt, lithium, and nickel production is geographically concentrated, giving import-dependent countries a strategic reason to recycle.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Battery-metal recycling is a supply-security play rather than a scarcity play, which means its value is tied to trade policy and import-dependence risk premia, not to depletion timelines.
insights.quote: While we are not about to run out of any of these materials globally in a strict sense, their supplies are limited in practical terms.
insights.locator: Are we running out of materials?

insights.claim: There is no material-scarcity case for recycling paper or glass: trees can be regrown (and growing them removes atmospheric carbon), and the silicon used to make glass is among the most abundant elements on Earth.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Paper and glass kerbside streams are the most exposed to a future policy rethink; municipal recycling contractors leveraged to those volumes carry unpriced regulatory risk.
insights.quote: The silicon used to make glass is one of the most abundant elements on Earth.
insights.locator: By contrast, there is no danger of running

themes.theme: Plastic feedstock is a byproduct, not a scarce resource

insights.claim: American plastic is made from ethane extracted from natural gas, and one kilogram of ethane left in the gas stream and burned for electricity would power a typical US house for only a few hours — versus becoming 100 shopping bags — while US proven shale gas reserves could last nearly a century at current rates.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: US plastics are an ultra-low-opportunity-cost use of NGL byproducts, so feedstock-driven cost advantage for US petrochemical crackers persists regardless of recycling policy.
insights.quote: One kilogram of ethane, left in the stream and made into electricity, could power a typical US house for a few hours, or it could be made into 100 shopping bags.
insights.locator: American plastic comes from ethane

insights.claim: A single 13-kilogram propane cylinder of the kind used for a gas grill contains enough feedstock for roughly 1,600 eight-gram carrier bags — about three years of a family's ten-bag weekly shop — which is why carrier bags remain extremely cheap.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Plastic packaging consumes a trivially small share of hydrocarbon volumes, so bans on it barely move oil demand — a reason to discount 'plastics phase-out' as a bear case for refiners.
insights.quote: One 13-kilogram propane cylinder, the kind a family might use to power their gas grill, could instead be made into about 1,600 typical eight-gram plastic carrier bags
insights.locator: The rest of the world makes plastics from

themes.theme: Contamination and yield loss break the recycling chain

insights.claim: Roughly 25 percent of items placed in American recycling bins are contaminants such as lids, food, or damp paper, and the true figure may be higher because most US states do not consistently track contamination data.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A quarter of input volume arriving as contamination means reported recycling rates overstate delivered material; underwrite MRF throughput on yield, not on collected tonnage.
insights.quote: About 25 percent of items placed in American recycling bins are contaminants
insights.locator: There ain’t no such thing as a free recycle

insights.claim: Public education programs have proven largely ineffective at reducing recycling contamination, and even cart tagging — the most forceful curbside method, where crews inspect bins and leave contaminated ones unemptied — cut contamination by only 29 percent over five rounds in an Oregon program.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Contamination is a structural ceiling that no behavioral intervention has cracked, so recycling-rate targets that assume improving input quality are likely to be missed.
insights.quote: a cart-tagging program in Oregon succeeded in reducing contamination by only 29 percent over five rounds
insights.locator: Reducing the contamination rate is challenging

insights.claim: Placing low-value plastics such as film, black food trays, bottle caps, and straws into a recycling bin can be actively harmful, because they are screened out and landfilled anyway while adding to contamination rates and to the labor and processing time required.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Well-intentioned consumer behavior degrades the economics of the very facilities it aims to support — a hidden opex drag on recycling infrastructure that policy rarely accounts for.
insights.locator: The imperfect recycling process means

insights.claim: Mid-value plastics such as the polypropylene in bottles and butter tubs need intensive washing that detaches recyclable fragments, then filtering, melting, and a second filtration before pelletizing, with yield losses as high as 45 percent.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Losing up to 45 percent of feed makes mechanical recycling of mid-grade resin structurally uncompetitive with virgin resin absent a large mandate or subsidy.
insights.quote: Yield losses can be as high as 45 percent.
insights.locator: Many mid-value plastics, like the polypropylene

themes.theme: Carbon abatement cost versus direct air capture

insights.claim: Recycling one ton of mid-quality tub-grade plastic avoids only 0.43 tons of CO2 versus virgin material while recycled tub-grade resin costs hundreds of dollars more per ton than virgin, implying consumers pay over $1,000 to abate one ton of carbon dioxide.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: This is an explicit implied carbon price for a widespread policy — any abatement option priced below roughly $1,000 per ton dominates it, which is the arbitrage a carbon-markets investor should watch.
insights.quote: This means that consumers are effectively paying over a thousand dollars to save one ton of carbon dioxide.
insights.locator: While the environmental case can hold up

insights.claim: Direct air capture currently averages about $490 per ton of CO2 removed, with specialists hoping to reach $100 per ton in coming decades — less than half, and potentially a tenth, of the implied cost of abating carbon through mid-grade plastic recycling.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: If waste budgets were reallocated on cost-per-ton logic, DAC and similar removal technologies would be the natural recipient — a demand-side catalyst for carbon-removal ventures.
insights.quote: direct air capture, which removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, currently costs an average of $490 per ton, and area specialists hope to lower the cost to $100 per ton in the coming decades
insights.locator: While the environmental case can hold up

themes.theme: Ocean plastic is a developing-world collection problem

insights.claim: Over 90 percent of waste in low-income countries is improperly managed and typically dumped, burned, or escapes into waterways, while richer countries have near-universal refuse collection and send almost none of their waste to the ocean.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on ocean plastic is basic collection infrastructure in poor countries, which redirects the impact case from Western consumer-goods reformulation to emerging-market waste capex.
insights.quote: In low-income countries, however, over 90 percent of waste is improperly managed
insights.locator: Richer countries have near-universal refuse collection

insights.claim: Approximately one hundred rivers, mostly in South and South-East Asia, account for half of ocean plastic, and a substantial share of ocean plastic is discarded fishing gear rather than household waste at all.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Extreme geographic and sectoral concentration means a small number of targeted interventions could deliver most of the benefit — high-leverage for impact capital and for ESG screens that currently target the wrong sources.
insights.quote: Approximately a hundred rivers, mostly in South and South-East Asia, account for half of ocean plastic.
insights.locator: Richer countries have near-universal refuse collection

insights.claim: Restrictions and disincentives on single-use plastics in Western countries are largely environmental theater, because in a Western country the choice between the recycling bin and general waste makes no difference to ocean litter — neither destination is the ocean.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Consumer-facing plastic bans generate compliance costs for packaged-goods and retail companies without addressing the stated harm, making them vulnerable to reversal or ridicule.
insights.quote: But much of this is environmental theater.
insights.locator: Your plastic toothbrush isn’t killing turtles

insights.claim: Modern landfills are built on thick clay layers and tough plastic liners, with waste placed in thin compacted covered layers, drainage pipes collecting and treating leachate, and long-term groundwater monitoring that continues after closure, making the image of an open leaching pit decades out of date in the developed world.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The public perception gap around landfill quality is itself the mispricing — landfill operators face reputational rather than technical risk, and that gap can close as evidence circulates.
insights.locator: Landfill is pretty clean

insights.claim: Landfill gas wells typically capture around 75 percent of methane produced and sometimes as much as 95 percent, routing it to flares or generators instead of the atmosphere.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Landfill gas capture at 75-95 percent turns the headline methane objection into a solved engineering problem and supports landfill-gas-to-energy as a monetizable asset class.
insights.quote: This typically captures around 75 percent of the methane produced, and sometimes as much as 95 percent.
insights.locator: Operators place waste in thin layers

insights.claim: New York's environmental regulator reviewed groundwater monitoring for 31 post-1988 landfills covering roughly 450 collective operating years and found no adverse impact on groundwater quality, with most documented leakage coming from legacy sites that had poorer liner systems.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A regulator's own dataset separating legacy from modern liner performance is the strongest available evidence for reclassifying landfill risk — relevant to remediation liability estimates.
insights.quote: found no adverse impact on groundwater quality
insights.locator: Operators place waste in thin layers

insights.claim: Controlled incineration contains methane better than landfill and can generate electricity from waste heat, but landfill is reliably 20-30 percent cheaper in the US and modern incinerators are among the most expensive power plants to build per megawatt, in some cases costing an order of magnitude more than a conventional natural gas plant.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Waste-to-energy capex per megawatt makes it structurally uncompetitive without a mandate, so municipal WTE projects depend on policy support rather than merchant power economics.
insights.quote: modern incinerators are among the most expensive power plants to build per megawatt, in some cases costing an order of magnitude more than a conventional natural gas plant
insights.locator: Out of the garbage can, into the fire

insights.claim: Incinerator cost is driven by chemistry: flue gas contains mercury, lead, and acid gases requiring expensive pollution control, and the acid gases would dissolve ordinary steel, so boilers must be lined with specialized ceramics or nickel-chromium alloy.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The cost driver is materials science, not scale, so waste-to-energy capex is unlikely to fall with deployment volume — a reason to doubt learning-curve projections for the sector.
insights.quote: The acid gases produced would dissolve normal steel, so the boilers have to be lined with either specialized ceramics or a nickel-chromium alloy.
insights.locator: This is because burning trash comes with

insights.claim: Around 500 million tons of waste are recycled globally each year, US recycling rates have more than tripled since 1980, and close to 50 percent of all EU waste is now recycled — yet expanding these rates further is unnecessary and will make societies poorer over time.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to targets embedded in major international environmental strategies; if this view gains traction, recycling-volume-linked business models face a demand ceiling.
insights.quote: Yet this is unnecessary and will make us poorer in the long run.
insights.locator: It’s okay to be a landfiller

insights.claim: Landfill land use is negligible — less than 0.01 percent of the United States, less than 0.001 percent of Australia, and about 0.02 percent of Germany — and closed landfills can be built on, so the land is not permanently consumed.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The 'we are running out of space' argument for diversion targets is quantitatively false in major developed markets, removing a key justification for recycling mandates.
insights.quote: less than 0.01 percent of the US is used for landfill, less than 0.001 percent of Australia is, and only about 0.02 percent of Germany is
insights.locator: In the developed world, though there are benefits

insights.claim: Metal recycling should likely be the primary or even exclusive focus of municipal recycling programs, with money currently spent on other streams redirected to measures such as carbon capture and to tighter monitoring and penalties for substandard landfill operators.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A concrete policy reallocation blueprint: long scrap-metal and carbon-removal exposure, short the assumption that multi-stream municipal recycling volumes keep growing.
insights.quote: The main exception is metal recycling, which should likely be the primary or even exclusive focus of municipal recycling programs.
insights.locator: Instead of paying more to recycle

insights.claim: Recycling is fragile because it requires simultaneous coordination of collection, separation, contamination control, and reliable buyers, and fails if any single link breaks, whereas landfill is simple and cheap — meaning even suboptimal landfill is an upgrade wherever the alternative is open dumping or burning.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Chain-fragility versus simplicity is the core investment lens: in emerging markets, basic landfill capex delivers far more environmental return per dollar than recycling infrastructure.
insights.quote: Recycling is complex to sustain: it requires the successful coordination of collection, separation, contamination control, and reliable buyers for the material. If even one part of the chain breaks down, it doesn’t work.
insights.locator: There is a great humanitarian and environmental case
